November 8, 2026




 JPL new boys Tru-Juice beat champions Portmore to retake lead 







ST CATHERINE, Jamaica – Debutants Tru-Juice FC handed Portmore United their first loss of the Legend Jamaica Premier League season, holding off the defending champions 2-1 at Ferdie Neita Park on Sunday.

It is a fourth straight win for Tru-Juice as they raced to 20 points atop the JPL table, two more than second-placed Waterhouse FC who will play on Monday evening, with Racing United and Montego bay United tied on 16 points, two more than Mount Pleasant FA who beat Tivoli Gardens 2-1 to open their new facility in St Ann.

Alex Marshall gave Tru-Juice the lead in the 41st minute with his second goal of the season, while Tyrone Mullings scored his league leading eighth goal in the 60th minute to double the lead.

Marques Reid scored for Portmore United in the 68th minute but they were unable to close the gap any further and stayed in eighth place on 10 points.

Montego Bay United came from two goals down to play out a 2-2 draw against 12th place Molynes United at Jarrett Park, extending their winless run to four games. Tyrique Wilson gave Molynes the lead in the fifth minute and Rashawn Livingston added a second in the 10th but Jourdain Fletcher in the 28th minute and Devontae Campbell in the 40th minute cancelled the lead.

Molynes United’s Raheem Porter (left) shields the ball from Montego Bay United’s Jesus Gudino in their Legend JPL first round game played at Jarrett Park on Sunday, November 8, 2026.. Montego Bay United rallied from two goals down to earn a 2-2 draw.
(Photo: Paul Reid)

Molynes, taking orders for the first time from new coach Anthony Patrick, and who had lost their two previous games, got off to a fast start and were rewarded when Wilson’s free kick from about 22 yards went under the MBU wall and beat goalkeeper Davonnie Burton at his right post.

Livingston doubled the lead when he finished off a good move with a low hard shot from the right side into the far corner of the MBU goal.

Richardo Ramsey, who replaced Javon Gordon after 25 minutes, set up MBU’s first goal when he blocked a pass from a Molynes defender and Fletcher was given a chance to run at the goal and beat goalkeeper Jason Belfon and cut the deficit in the 28th minute.

Campbell brought the home team level when he dribbled from about 40 yards and gave Belfon no chance from close range.

Fletcher should have scored a third for MBU but his volley from inside the 18-yard box was wide of the target.

MBU dominated the game in the second half but just failed to get the winner with Ramsey redirecting a low hard cross over the cross bar from about a yard out late in the game.

Mount Pleasant opened their new facility with a come-from-behind win over Tivoli Gardens who took the lead in the 23rd minute through Mickel Graham.

Warner Brown equalised in the 53rd minute and Nickalia Fuller came off the bench to score the winner in the 70th minute.

Dunbeholden FC scored a late equaliser to get a 1-1 draw against Treasure Beach at the STETHS Sports Complex in Santa Cruz.

Daniel Hardy gave Treasure Beach the lead in the 74th minute but Nevaun Turner scored late, in time added, to give his team a share of the points.

Cavalier FC led Humble Lion 1-0 in their game at Effortville when it was called off with 15 minutes to be played due to heavy rain,

 Family seeking help to locate missing ‘mentally-challenged’ woman 







ST JAMES, Jamaica — A St James family is seeking the public’s help in locating a relative who has gone missing.

The missing woman is 36-year- old Rushelle Gordon, fondly called “Neeky”, who has been missing since Thursday, November 5.

Reports are that the woman and her mother were travelling in a taxi along Orange Street in the vicinity of Paradise Row when the vehicle stopped to allow two passengers to get off. 

The woman had to come off to allow the passengers off. However, when the passengers came off, the driver drove off without the woman.

The car went a distance before her mother managed to disembark just around the corner and by the time she returned to the area where her daughter was, she was missing.

The daughter is nonverbal and, according to her family, has mental challenges which impacts her decision making.

She is dark complexion, medium built and is 5ft 6inches tall.

Information coming forward is that she was last seen in the Railway Lane/market area of Montego Bay after family members showed images of her in the area.

The police have been alerted and are actively trying to locate the woman.

news.title: India could benefit from US midterm outcome via lower oil prices and yields: Axis MF
news.text: New Delhi India could emerge as one of the key beneficiaries of a changing global investment environment following the US midterm election results, with the possibility of lower crude oil prices, softer global bond yields and improved foreign investment flows, according to a report by Axis Mutual Fund. In the latest November 2026 US midterm elections, the Democratic Party won control of both the Senate and the House of Representatives, delivering a significant political setback to President Donald Trump’s administration. The report said the Democratic gains in the US Congress could increase legislative checks on the administration over the remaining two years of the US President’s term, potentially creating room for a more measured approach towards geopolitical tensions, tariffs and financial conditions. The Democrats have indicated that affordability, the conflict with Iran and tariffs will receive greater attention when the new Congress takes charge in January. Axis Mutual Fund said the changed political balance could ease some near-term global economic pressures, although it does not guarantee a return to the global economic and geopolitical conditions that existed before the current period of disruption. “The result may create some room for a more measured approach to geopolitical tensions, tariffs and financial conditions,” the report said. One of the biggest potential benefits for global markets could come from lower crude oil prices if geopolitical tensions in West Asia ease. A reduction in crude prices could also help moderate inflationary pressures and reduce the pressure on global bond yields. The report said India could particularly benefit from such a situation as it is a major importer of both energy and capital. High oil prices, elevated US yields and a strong US dollar have together created a challenging environment for emerging markets, affecting currencies and capital flows. “India could benefit from a softer crude and yields environment because it is a major importer of both energy and capital,” the report said. According to the report, a sustained decline in crude prices could improve India’s trade balance, reduce dollar demand and ease pressure on the balance of payments and the rupee. If accompanied by softer US bond yields, it could also create a more favourable environment for foreign portfolio investment flows into Indian markets. Lower energy costs could also reduce imported inflation, transportation expenses and input costs for businesses. This may improve household purchasing power and corporate profit margins while providing greater flexibility for monetary policy. For the stock market, the report expects a possible broadening of market leadership, with consumption-oriented businesses, financial companies and other interest-rate-sensitive sectors potentially benefiting from lower input costs and softer yields. However, the report cautioned that attractive valuations alone may not be enough to support a sustained recovery in stock prices, as an improvement in earnings growth would remain important. The report also highlighted that changes in US political leadership are unlikely to reverse long-term global trends such as strategic competition between the US and China, supply-chain restructuring and investment in critical minerals and technology.
news.summary: Democratic gains may ease geopolitical tensions and support FPI flows, though earnings growth remains key for markets

news.title: Brent oil futures flat after Trump’s remarks on Iran war
news.text: Mangaluru, November 9 Brent crude oil futures traded flat on Monday morning despite a statement by US President Donald Trump on the war with Iran. At 9.33 am on Monday, January Brent oil futures were at $98.31, down by 0.01 per cent, and December crude oil futures on WTI (West Texas Intermediate) were at $91.31, up by 0.53 per cent. November crude oil futures were trading at ₹8569 on the Multi Commodity Exchange (MCX) during the initial hour of trading on Monday against the previous close of ₹8554, up by 0.18 per cent, and December futures were trading at ₹8480 against the previous close of ₹8478, up by 0.02 per cent. Trump told CNN that he was unlikely to order fresh attacks on Iran as long as talks to end the war progress. “It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement. The answer is: highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary,” Trump told CNN in a phone interview. In a post on Truth Social, he said: “Task Force Iron Gate is in full force and effect in the Islamic Republic of Iran. Coupled with history’s greatest Naval Blockade, very little gets into, or out of, Iran!” An Al Jazeera report, which quoted Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein, said Iraq reached an understanding with the US to allow ⁠Iraqi oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz via a shipping lane near Oman. The Minister said Iraq has suffered around $60 billion in losses due to the Iran war and disruptions to oil exports. Meanwhile, reports said the Houthis conducted an attack on Saudi Arabia’s Riyadh on Sunday. According to the reports, the attack damaged Saudi Aramco’s offices in Riyadh.

news.title: Nifty slips below 25,000 as IT, power stocks drag; banks, pharma hold firm
news.text: Markets opened on a cautious note Monday morning, with the benchmark Nifty 50 declining 30.40 points, or 0.12 per cent, to trade at 24,956 as of 9.29 am, after closing at 24,986.40 on Sunday's Muhurat trading session. The Sensex, which had closed at 80,999.40, opened at 81,327.29 but quickly retreated to 80,938.76, down 60.64 points or 0.07 per cent, as profit-booking emerged following a sharp rally last week. https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/topic/nifty/ https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/topic/sensex/ State Bank of India led gains among Nifty50 constituents, rising 1.82 per cent to ₹1,034.45 from its previous close of ₹1,016, on volumes of 49.10 lakh shares worth ₹506.18 crore. Apollo Hospitals advanced 1.09 per cent to ₹8,521.50 against a previous close of ₹8,430, while Dr. Reddy's Laboratories gained 1.07 per cent to ₹1,384.70 from ₹1,370. ICICI Bank rose 0.99 per cent to ₹1,580.50 from ₹1,565, clocking volumes worth ₹733.35 crore, among the heaviest traded on the index. HDFC Bank added 0.91 per cent to ₹791.20 from ₹784.10, with over 154 lakh shares changing hands worth ₹1,226.12 crore. https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/stocks/state-bank-of-india/ On the losing side, HCL Technologies fell the most, dropping 1.50 per cent to ₹1,420.40 from its previous close of ₹1,442. Power Grid Corporation declined 1.24 per cent to ₹258.10 from ₹261.35, while Bharti Airtel shed 1.21 per cent to ₹2,060.20 from ₹2,085.50 on volumes worth ₹150 crore. Hindalco Industries slipped 1.01 per cent to ₹943.40 from ₹953, and Nestle India fell 0.93 per cent to ₹1,261.60 from ₹1,273.50. https://www.thehindubusinessline.com/stocks/hcl-technologies-ltd/ The morning's mixed picture follows a week in which the Nifty surged 8.5 per cent and the Bank Nifty climbed 7.5 per cent. Shrikant Chouhan, Head of Equity Research at Kotak Neo, noted that both indices have crossed critical swing levels. "Sustaining above these levels could gradually open the upside towards the next major hurdles at 26,000–26,350 for the Nifty and 85,000–85,900 for the Bank Nifty," he said, adding that "periodic corrections or pullbacks towards key retracement levels and major moving-average supports would be healthy and could provide fresh entry opportunities." Foreign institutional investors have been a key driver of the recent rally, with FIIs pumping ₹13,749.82 crore into Indian equities on November 6. Dr. V K Vijayakumar, Chief Investment Strategist at Geojit Investments, attributed the sustained buying to a confluence of factors. "FII allocations track index weights during major market shifts," he said, pointing to fair valuations, declining crude prices and improving corporate earnings as among the triggers. "The Democrat's victory in the US elections...caused fears of deceleration in AI spending and sharp correction in AI stocks," he noted, which redirected flows toward emerging markets including India. Bank Nifty, currently at 58,850.65, broke above its previous major high of 58,706 set in June 2026. Sachin Gupta, VP of Technical Research at Choice Equity Broking, flagged that "sustained strength above the upper end likely to support further upside," with the immediate range pegged at 58,500–59,500. ICICI Bank, which had surged 4.75 per cent in Friday's session, continued to anchor private banking gains. On the global front, US markets provided a mixed cue, with the Nasdaq gaining 1.09 per cent and the S&P 500 rising 0.31 per cent on Friday, while the Dow Jones slipped 0.46 per cent. Asian markets were also split, with Japan's Nikkei 225 up over 1 per cent and South Korea's KOSPI lower by more than 0.50 per cent. Crude oil at around $90 per barrel and diplomatic signals from US President Donald Trump indicating military strikes on Iran as "highly unlikely" if negotiations progress have provided some comfort to energy-sensitive sectors. Ponmudi R, CEO of Enrich Money, cautioned that "Thursday's CPI data...could provide the next significant directional cue for domestic equities," even as a firming rupee and stable crude continue to support sentiment. Pabitro Mukherjee, Deputy Vice President of Research at Bajaj Broking, highlighted the speed of the market's recovery. The Nifty has "completely retraced its 9 weeks decline from 24,774 to 22,179 in just 5 weeks," he said, adding that "a faster retracement of the previous major decline in almost half the time interval signals strength." He pegged the next upside targets at 25,400 and 25,800, with immediate support at 24,700.

news.title: Trump says his immigration policy 'too tough' after midterm drubbing
news.text: Washington US President Donald Trump acknowledged that his immigration policy was “too tough” after a severe drubbing in the midterm elections and said he was ready to work with the Democratic Party in the years ahead. Democrats won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the November 3 midterm elections, flipping several Republican-held seats in a sweeping setback for Trump. The results reflected voter dissatisfaction with his handling of the immigration issue, the economy, the Iran war and rising living costs. “I think it was too tough. I think it might be too tough,” Trump told CBS' 60 Minutes in response to a question on his administration's deportation policy. The interview was recorded on Friday and telecast on Sunday evening. Soon after the interview was recorded, Trump appointed Stephen Miller, known for his strong views against immigration, as his Chief of Staff, raising questions about whether the president would significantly soften his approach. Indian tech workers were among those worst affected by the hard-line immigration policies pursued by the Trump administration. Asked about the reasons for Republicans' resounding defeat, Trump echoed the conventional wisdom that it was due to the Iran war and gas prices, while also pointing to hostility towards Israel as a factor. “They didn’t like the war,” Trump said. “They didn’t like the fact that gasoline went up because I had it down at a low. And there’s a great dislike, incredibly, for Israel.” The president said his immigration crackdown had "both helped and hurt" him at the polls. Trump said he believed he "got an A+ for closing up the border" and "very high marks for getting the bad ones out". "But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs, that created one violation, or breaking of the law, and that was that they came into the country illegally," he said. "Now, there is a large part of the country that thinks that they should be put out. And there's a large part of the country that thinks that they should be allowed to stay if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes. "I think it was too tough," the Republican leader reiterated. Trump also repeated his claim that he had prevented a nuclear war between India and Pakistan. “I've settled eight wars. I settled eight wars. I mean, India-Pakistan would've been a nuclear war. I got it settled before it got going. “They had 11 planes shot down. They were ready to go. The prime minister of Pakistan said, 'Trump saved 30-50 million lives.' I settled a lot of wars,” he said. India launched Operation Sindoor on May 7, 2025, targeting terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir (PoK) following the April 22 terror attack in Pahalgam that claimed 26 lives. New Delhi has consistently rejected Trump's claims of US mediation, maintaining that the understanding to cease military action was worked out directly between the two countries' Directors General of Military Operations on May 10, 2025. India has also said that no trade-related discussions took place with the US during the conflict. Asked what he thought would happen after his death, Trump said, “I hope I'm missed.” He also described himself as a “religious person” and said he hoped to go to heaven.
news.summary: “I think it was too tough. I think it might be too tough,” Trump told CBS' 60 Minutes in response to a question on his administration's deportation policy

news.title: Trump says likely to meet Putin, Xi in China
news.text:
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump said Sunday he would likely be meeting with the leaders of Russia and China next week to discuss ending the Iran war.

Trump told reporters he expects to meet with Xi Jinping of China and Vladimir Putin of Russia at an Asia-Pacific summit in Shenzhen, China scheduled for November 18-19.

“Well, I’m going to be going to China,” Trump said, “and one of the meetings I think will be with President Putin and President Xi, and that’ll be interesting.”

He added: “We’ll talk a lot of things, including denuclearization, but we’ll be talking a lot of things. We’re trying to end the war in Iran.”

The Kremlin said October 21 that this first of its kind trilateral meeting is “being prepared.”

This followed a Wall Street Journal report that Putin wanted the three-way talks to broker a peace deal in Ukraine that would be favorable to Moscow, which invaded Ukraine in 2022.

Trump is criticized in the United States as having a fondness for authoritarian leaders like those of China and Russia, among others.

Trump’s willingness to meet with Putin is a further show of how the US president has worked to end the international isolation of Russia that was triggered by its invasion.
news.summary: President Donald Trump announced plans to meet with Russian and Chinese leaders at the Asia-Pacific summit in China to discuss the Iran war.

news.title: The Kremlin hopes the US election shake-up won't shift Trump's negotiations on Ukraine
news.text: The Republicans' defeat in the U.S. midterm elections was watched closely in Russia, where some observers are predicting it could herald more support for Ukraine when the Democrats take over Congress in January.But if the Kremlin is hearing the ticking of a clock on its nearly 5-year-old full-scale invasion of its neighbor, it seemingly remains unperturbed.Asked if the election's outcome could stymie U.S. attempts to help negotiate a settlement between Moscow and Kyiv, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov voiced hope that U.S. President Donald Trump will continue to pursue his peace efforts.'There is groundwork already in place, and another round of trilateral negotiations is set to take place very soon,' Peskov said of talks planned for Tuesday and Wednesday involving Russian, Ukrainian and U.S. representatives in Abu Dhabi, United Arab Emirates.He also praised the 'successful humanitarian peace-building efforts' by first lady Melania Trump, adding that 'we hope that all of this will continue.' Last week's limited ceasefire around the Russia-occupied city of Oleshky, brokered with her help, allowed for the delivery of humanitarian aid and the evacuation of some residents.Peskov shrugged off a question from reporters on whether the new Congress would challenge Trump's stance on Russia and Ukraine. He called it an 'internal matter' for the U.S.Trump's recent moves have appeared to favor MoscowLast month, he struck a diesel fuel import deal with Russia in a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on the Kremlin, to the dismay of Ukraine and its European allies. He also claimed that Kyiv's attacks on Russian oil refineries caused a spike in diesel prices in the U.S. He urged Kyiv to halt the strikes, even though rising global energy prices were largely driven by the Iran war.Trump also issued an executive order to put on hold sweeping new sanctions that clamped down on the Russian economy, telling Congress the pause was in the national interest. Lawmakers from both parties blasted Trump's move as benefiting Russian President Vladimir Putin.At the same time, Ukraine reported a throttling of Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service owned by Elon Musk's SpaceX. Trump denied being behind the brief slowing of Starshield, but the move to limit the system that serves as the backbone of Ukraine's drone operations and battlefield communications was widely seen as part of Washington's efforts to pressure Kyiv.The diesel deal appeared to falter this week after U.S. federal and state officials warned that handling any shipments could bring legal consequences, and two U.S.-bound tankers changed course. The Kremlin sought to play down the development, saying deliveries will continue.Kyiv desperately needs to replenish its supplies of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors to fend off Russia's ballistic missile attacks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has made repeated requests for Washington to speed up delivery of the defensive systems, but U.S. stockpiles have been exhausted by the Iran war, and the U.S. has prioritized replenishing its own arsenals.On Oct. 30, the Trump administration said it has approved a proposed $2.1 billion sale of Patriot interceptors for Ukraine after Kyiv had accused the Pentagon of delaying delivery.Trump also appeared to echo the Kremlin's view that Zelenskyy was an obstacle to peace while saying Putin was more open to a deal.Trump on Thursday conferred with Putin's envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who attended a White House ceremony with the first lady recognizing last week's humanitarian truce. The president didn't meet any of the Ukrainian officials also at the event but hinted that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works.Many in Russia argue that the Democrats' victory could put congressional pressure on Trump to tread more carefully and toughen his stand on Russia.Dmitry Medvedev, who served as Russian president in 2008-12, predicted that Trump would be less inclined to press Ukraine when a new Congress is seated.'He doesn't need an extra confrontation with Democrats,' said Medvedev, who now serves as deputy head of Russia's Security Council.The new House and Senate could boost aid to UkraineThere has been strong bipartisan support for Ukraine, raising the prospect of veto-proof passage of more aid to Kyiv or tough new sanctions on Moscow.On Wednesday, Zelenskyy told German broadcaster ZDF that while there has been backing for Kyiv from both parties, the Democrats 'speak very clearly about supporting Ukraine.'In other remarks Thursday, the Ukrainian leader also noted the midterm elections could have a positive effect on U.S. assistance, including speedier delivery of the Patriot interceptors. 'I believe our chances of getting additional assistance from the United States may now grow,' he said.Abbas Gallyamov, a former Putin speechwriter-turned-political analyst who lives abroad, argued that his old boss had missed a chance of striking a deal on Ukraine before the Democrats won and now could face a less cooperative Washington.'Putin's prospects have significantly worsened,' Gallyamov wrote in a commentary. 'He thought that the time was on his side and wasn't in a hurry to use the window of opportunity that had opened after Trump's victory, and now this window is starting to close.'Some policy experts, however, cautioned against expectations of a dramatic shift.The Democrats could put more funding for Ukraine on the agenda and increase pressure on Trump over the diesel deal or Russia sanctions waivers, but hard limits on the president's power are unlikely, said Jorn Fleck, senior director of the Atlantic Council's Europe Center.'Even with a strong majority in both chambers of Congress, Democrats will struggle to impose meaningful limits on Trump's conduct of foreign policy, given his constitutional powers and willingness to push the envelope,' Fleck said in a commentary. 'Unshackled from having to face voters at the ballot box again, Trump may shift into deal-making overdrive to cement his legacy.'Some expect a more hard-line TrumpKonstantin Kosachev, a deputy speaker of the upper house of the Russian parliament, argued that Trump's executive powers in the foreign policy sphere would allow him to pursue his course regardless of congressional opposition.He said if authorities in Kyiv believed that the Republicans' defeat would make the Trump administration more receptive to Ukraine's requests, they could be mistaken.'They will not find a more pliable or constrained Trump,' Kosachev said. 'Rather, they will face a more resolute one, who is no longer looking over his shoulder at upcoming elections.'For all the importance of Congress, 'the U.S. president's role in foreign policy remains paramount — a fact Trump understands better than anyone else,' he said.Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna struck a similar tone in an interview Thursday with The Associated Press, saying 'the president is President Trump,' and he has the ability to dictate foreign and security policy. 'Unpredictability' should be expected, he added.Kosachev said that by pinning their hopes on a victory by the Democrats, Kyiv and its allies in London, Brussels and other capitals in Europe have sided with Trump's domestic political adversaries.'Consequently, they are all but guaranteed two years of a hard-line Trump,' he said.

news.title: Renewed US strikes on Iran ‘highly unlikely’ if negotiations progress: Trump
news.text:
Washington: US President Donald Trump said that renewed military strikes on Iran were “highly unlikely” as long as negotiations made progress, but did not rule out further military actions.

In a phone interview with CNN, Trump claimed Sunday that the United States had already dealt a severe blow to Iran and that further military action was “highly unlikely” to be necessary.

“It depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement,” Trump noted, referring to Iran’s nuclear program and the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.

The president also claimed that the United States had identified potential infrastructure targets in Iran, including power plants and bridges, and could destroy 38 bridges in an hour, Xinhua news agency reported.

“Most likely it will not be necessary,” Trump reiterated. “They want to make a deal so badly.”

Earlier Trump said that Washington was talking to Iran, as his administration imposed sanctions on eight Canadian businesses accused of helping Tehran move money through cryptocurrency networks.

“We’re talking to Iran. We have been,” Trump told reporters before departing the White House.

The president portrayed the military situation as favourable to the United States and said the Strait of Hormuz was opening.

“We’ve beaten Iran. We are doing very well with Iran,” he said.

Asked for his message to Iran, Trump combined his claim of military success with an indication that diplomatic contacts were continuing.

His comments came on the same day that the Treasury Department announced sanctions against eight Canada-based money services businesses under Operation Economic Outcast.

Treasury accused the companies of exchanging Iranian rials and other currencies for digital assets to facilitate international transactions involving Iran. It said many had dealt with sanctioned Iranian cryptocurrency exchanges or addresses associated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

More than eight months after the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran, Trump has repeatedly sent mixed signals about his willingness to end the conflict. Washington and Tehran remain at a stalemate, with little significant progress in diplomatic efforts.

news.title: Sensex, Nifty open higher amid positive global cues
news.text: Digital Desk | Mumbai, Nov 9 (IANS) Indian equity benchmarks opened higher on Monday, tracking positive global cues and gains in financial and banking stocks. Sensex gained 327.89 points or 0.4 per cent to open at 81,327.29, while Nifty rose 90 points or 0.36 per cent to 25,076.40. Sector-wise, the Nifty Financial Services 25/50 index led the gains, rising 0.57 per cent in early trade, followed by Nifty PSU Bank which advanced 0.47 per cent. Nifty Private Bank gained 0.37 per cent, while Nifty Healthcare Index rose 0.35 per cent. Nifty Metal and Nifty Pharma were up 0.33 per cent and 0.24 per cent, respectively. On the downside, Nifty IT declined 0.47 per cent, while Nifty MidSmall IT & Telecom fell 0.39 per cent. Market experts said the strong rally last week had significantly improved investor sentiment, supported by a rare convergence of favourable factors, including aggressive FII buying, attractive valuations, easing crude oil prices, declining US bond yields and improving corporate earnings as reflected in the second-quarter results. “Concerns over a slowdown in artificial intelligence (AI) spending and a sharp correction in AI-related stocks also contributed to the shift in global market dynamics,” they said. The experts said FII buying in India is likely to sustain, potentially paving the way for further gains in large-cap stocks. They added that foreign investor allocations tend to track index weights during major market shifts. Apart from that, the domestic market sentiment remained upbeat following a strong rally last week, with the Nifty surging 8.6 per cent amid sustained foreign institutional investor (FII) buying and improving global cues. Globally, US equities ended higher in the previous session, with the Nasdaq gaining 1.09 per cent and the S&P 500 advancing 0.31 per cent. US equity futures and Asian markets edged higher on Monday, stabilising after a volatile week during which concerns over chip demand triggered sharp losses across technology-heavy Asian markets. In addition, crude oil prices opened lower on Monday after US President Donald Trump indicated that further strikes on Iran were unlikely as peace talks progressed.

news.title: Trump says his deportation policy ‘might have been too tough’ for voters
news.text:
President Donald Trump in his first major interview since his party lost control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections said he thinks his administration was too aggressive on deportations.

He also said he thinks he can work with Democrats in the new Congress on some kind of immigration deal.

Mr Trump said his deportation policy was part of the reason Republicans lost, telling CBS’s 60 Minutes programme in an interview that aired on Sunday: “I think it might be too tough, yeah.”

He added that he thinks he could reach an agreement with the new Democratic majority.

“The deal would be we would work something out,” he said.

“And I think it’s something — I think that’s something that’s actually doable.”

Mr Trump did not give specifics about what that deal would look like — and shortly after taping the interview on Friday, Mr Trump named the key architect of his hard-line immigration agenda, Stephen Miller, as his new chief of staff.

“Trump says his immigration crackdown went too far,” Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer scoffed on social media on Sunday after the interview aired.

“Apparently, his solution was to put the man responsible for it in charge of the White House. That’s not a course correction. That’s a promotion.”

The president’s immigration crackdown was a prominent feature of his return to office with major operations in multiple cities sending arrests soaring.

Two US citizens — Renee Good and Alex Pretti — were killed by federal officers during protests against the operations.

Democrats have said oversight of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (Ice) and the Department of Homeland Security is a priority for the new Congress.

Mr Trump said he believes that “killers” and “drug dealers” in the country illegally should be deported, but suggested he was open to the idea of a deal that would let others stay “if they’re good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes”.

On the race among Republicans to succeed him for the 2028 presidential election, Mr Trump hinted at staying neutral.

Asked whether he would endorse a potential successor, the president said: “Probably, not necessarily.

“We have a tremendous bench. I have so many people that I have great relationships with.”

Asked about possible candidates other than vice-president JD Vance, Mr Trump only named Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is viewed as a possible 2028 contender.

“I think Marco’s great,” Mr Trump said.

“But there are many others and I’d rather not mention their names. There’s some senators that are excellent. I know ’em all, I like ’em a lot.

“So I may or may not get involved. I don’t know. Maybe I’m better off not getting involved.”
news.author: Mike Catalini

news.text: Sen. Bernie Sanders said Democrats should hold President Donald Trump accountable after taking control of the House and Senate in January, but warned the party not to spend too much time on probing the president and his allies. During an appearance on NBC News' "Meet the Press," the senator said it is still important to investigate Trump administration officials for alleged corruption and illegal activity, but stressed that the priority should be tackling affordability and supporting working-class families. Asked by host Kristen Welker if he believes that spending two years investigating Trump and his officials could jeopardize the mandate to lower prices and make life more affordable, Sanders replied, "Yes, I do." news.title: Trump Makes Bonkers Admission About Press Secretary Fiasco
news.text:
President Donald Trump has been cornered over his wild suggestion that UFC CEO Dana White could be his replacement press secretary.

Trump, 80, made the bizarre suggestion on his Truth Social account on Saturday, claiming he had offered his friend White, 57, the public-facing job that Katie Zacharia left after just five days.

“We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left,” Trump wrote in his post. “Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!”

The president also named, and shared photos of, six UFC fighters he suggested White could hire as his “assistants,” noting that some of them are “not from our Country,” to defend MAGA against the “Lunatic Left.” Trump previously recruited White to stage a UFC fight at the White House for his 80th birthday.

Trump’s post sparked online confusion over whether the president’s team had actually suggested Dana W. White, who previously worked as the Pentagon’s chief spokesperson, for the White House job, instead.

However, Dana W. White promptly rejected the suggestion in a LinkedIn post addressing the confusion. “It is nice for once that, that Dana White is being confused with this Dana White,” she wrote.

Meanwhile, the UFC boss appeared to play down the possibility when asked about Trump’s post at a news conference on Saturday, saying he already had a “lot of jobs.” He said he was due to meet Trump at the White House on Monday.

Trump added to the speculation on Sunday by sharing a cartoon video depicting White as press secretary, flanked by UFC fighters who attack reporters during a mock White House briefing.

Speaking to reporters before flying out of Florida on Sunday to return to the White House, Trump was asked if he was “serious” or “kidding around” about recruiting the UFC CEO as his new spokesperson.

Trump began his explanation by pointing to the “rough faces” of the fighters on his Truth Social post.

“You would have thought that people would have said, ‘He’s having a good time,’” Trump admitted. “I will tell you, I was only kidding.”

However, he insisted, “Dana loves the idea and there’s only one Dana. He’s great. I don’t know. He would be... you wouldn’t mess around with him so much. But so, I was kidding, of course.”

He then doubled down on his punchline, saying, “When you look at the fighters that I put in, that’s why I said some don’t come from our country. They come from parts unknown. They come from, uh, a lot of areas that are very rough areas.”

Trump’s list included two athletes from Russia’s Dagestan region, Islam Makhachev and Khabib Nurmagomedov and Amanda Nunes, a Brazilian native who became a U.S. citizen last year, as well as Americans Justin Gaethje, Daniel Cormier and “Kayla Harris,” which was most likely a reference to U.S. judo gold medalist Kayla Harrison.

“So I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea and he is a very capable guy... ”

He continued to explain the joke that many people missed, saying, “Of course I was kidding, and you could see that, because I put all of the great fighters as his assistants, that they’re all going to come with him. But uh, it was it was just a little fun.”

Trump said White would visit him in Washington on Monday for “other reasons,” adding that his post “was an example of something where I was kidding and then people said, ‘You know, that’s actually a pretty good idea’.”

Trump did not name anyone who approved of his idea.

CNN’s Kaitlan Collins and Isabelle D’Antonio reported that a source familiar with the matter said White had declined the offer. 

Talk show host and Trump foe Rosie O’Donnell seized on the president’s post before he clarified he was not serious.

“I thought this was fake — apparently it’s not—he [thinks] the UFC — run by Dana White is going to save his fetid a-- —#25thamendmentnow — he has lost his f---ing mind completely #gethimout,” she wrote on social media on Sunday, later posting it again, stating “Just gonna leave this here #dumba--.”

The Daily Beast has contacted the White House for comment.

Trump, 80, made the bizarre suggestion on his Truth Social account on Saturday, claiming he had offered his friend White, 57, the public-facing job that Katie Zacharia left after just five days.

news.title: Trump says 'a lot of people didn't like' Vance's criticism of Iran war after crushing midterm defeat... but challenges vice president to answer one question
news.text:
President Donald Trump has claimed that 'a lot of people' were unhappy with JD Vance's criticism of the Iran war, while revealing the one question he wants his vice president to answer after Republicans suffered a crushing midterm election defeat.

Trump insisted his relationship with Vance remained strong despite the vice president publicly blaming the eight-month conflict for the party's disastrous election performance.

But speaking to reporters before boarding Air Force One back to Washington D.C. on Sunday night, the president said Vance had failed to make one crucial point: whether he would still support going to war with Iran if given the opportunity to make the decision again.

Asked whether Vance's comments questioning the administration's decisions had damaged their relationship, Trump was adamant.

'No, not at all. But a lot of people didn't like his comments, but not me,' the president insisted.

'He was right other than one thing,' Trump continued, arguing that Vance should have addressed whether the controversial military campaign had been worth launching.

'If you had to do it again, would you do it again? The answer is "yes",' Trump said.

'I can tell you if I had to do it again this historically, for history this will go down as one of the best things we ever did because if they ever had a nuclear weapon, they would blow up the world - you know why? 'Cause they're crazy.'

The exchange came just hours after Trump was pressed about the same issue during a wide-ranging interview with CBS 60 Minutes, in which he acknowledged that Vance's assessment of the Republican defeat was not necessarily wrong.

Trump appeared determined to play down suggestions of a rift during the interview.

When correspondent Ross Douthat asked whether he agreed with Vance's analysis of the election, including his criticism of America's relationship with Israel, Trump replied: 'I don't disagree.'

The president then returned to the question he believed his vice president had failed to answer on the Iran War.

'The only thing I wish he would've said there, if he felt it and you'd have to ask him about that, but "If you had to do it again, would you do it?",' Trump said.

'You know he was part of a decision-making process and my answer is an emphatic "yes" because you can't let Iran have a nuclear weapon.'

Trump acknowledged that the decision might not appear politically advantageous in the short term but insisted history would ultimately vindicate him.

'I think historically this will be a very good decision. Is it a good decision for today and tomorrow? Maybe not, but you know I have to go with what's right for our country,' he said.

The president maintained that allowing Iran to obtain a nuclear weapon would have been a far greater failure.

Vance, who is widely regarded as a potential contender for the 2028 Republican presidential nomination, stunned political observers on Wednesday when he explicitly blamed the war for the GOP's loss of both chambers of Congress.

'The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,' Vance wrote in a lengthy post to X.

The vice president cited polling showing that Americans who supported Trump in 2024 had turned against Republicans over the conflict, rising living costs and Washington's relationship with Israel.

According to Vance, a pollster had identified four principal demands among disillusioned Trump voters: ending the war, tackling inflation, putting America First and changing America's relationship with Israel.

'Our voters showed up. And the above four reasons are why many of them voted for Democrats,' Vance wrote.

He also challenged those who believed the military campaign had been justified to acknowledge its devastating political consequences.

'If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so,' he declared. 'Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that's at least honest.'

The unusually direct assessment raised questions about whether the vice president was attempting to distance himself from Trump's increasingly unpopular foreign policy ahead of a possible presidential run.

Iran, meanwhile, has consistently maintained that its nuclear program is intended for peaceful purposes, although international inspectors have raised concerns about its stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

Diplomatic efforts have so far struggled to bring the conflict to a lasting resolution.

Trump has also warned that American forces have identified dozens of Iranian infrastructure targets, including 38 bridges, that could be struck if major hostilities resume.

US forces have continued conducting limited military operations, including strikes against Iranian air defenses, despite efforts to revive diplomacy.
news.summary: President Donald Trump admitted 'a lot of people' disliked JD Vance's criticism of the Iran war but insisted their relationship remained strong. Trump said his vice president was largely correct.

news.title: Trump backs US energy permitting reform bill ahead of key Senate vote
news.text: By Ari Natter A bipartisan plan to speed the federal approval process for major energy and infrastructure projects received the endorsement of President Donald Trump on the eve of a key Senate vote on the bill. “This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump said in a social media post Sunday that urged senators to vote in favor the bill. The Senate is slated Monday to take a procedural vote on the measure, seen as a once-in-a-generation chance to overhaul the byzantine system for approving projects needed to modernize power grids, build artificial-intelligence data centers and revitalize clean energy development. The legislation is supported from groups including oil companies and renewable energy developers, but faces hurdles to passage in the two remaining months Congress is in session. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is opposing the bill in its current form, arguing it hasn’t received enough input from House Democrats. Other progressive Democrats say they should use their newfound control of Congress next year to negotiate for a better deal. Democratic Senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich of New Mexico, as well as Republican Senators Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia and Mike Lee of Utah, unveiled a new version of the bill Saturday, but several environmental groups said they still opposed it. “After closely evaluating the full bill and the newly released substitute amendment alongside our state and territorial affiliates, Tribal partners, environmental justice partners, hunting, fishing, and outdoor recreation partners, water coalition partners, and other conservation partners, we have concluded we cannot support the legislation in its current form,” Collin O’Mara, president of the National Wildlife Federation said in a statement Sunday.
news.summary: Trump endorsed a bipartisan bill to speed up federal approvals for energy and infrastructure projects, urging senators to back the measure ahead of a procedural vote

news.title: Leaders gather in Turkey for UN climate summit after a disastrous year of extreme weather
news.text: ANTALYA: World leaders, delegates and climate activists on Monday will begin negotiations on curbing climate change, which in the last year has led to rising temperatures, deadly heat waves in Europe and beyond, and has played a role in disasters like the devastating floods in Nepal.This U.N. climate summit, called the Conference of the Parties, or COP31, also comes as the war in Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, pushing up global prices of gasoline and oil and myriad products made with them, such as fertilizers and pesticides. The disruption has pushed governments to rethink energy policies, both in the short-term and long-term, including increased investment in renewable energy sources like wind and solar.Delegates, meeting in the Turkish Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, will come under pressure to develop new pledges for climate action while implementing previous promises. The stakes are high: climate scientists say global average temperature rise will exceed 1.5 C (2.7 F) since the early 1800s.Limiting temperature rise to that threshold was a goal established during the 2015 Paris Agreement. Since then, it's been a focus of international climate negotiations. That the goal is no longer realistic underscores how difficult it's been for the world to cut greenhouse gas emissions, which are released into the atmosphere when fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal are burned, leading to climate change."This is the first COP where it is clear beyond a reasonable doubt that the world will overshoot the 1.5-degree target," said Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum. "We will not look away, and we will not lower our ambition."Kurum, the COP31 president, has said that rather than establishing new targets, he wants the summit to focus on turning previous climate commitments into action..Guterres declares Climate talks a 'Moment of Truth' as UN summit opens in Turkey .He has announced an "Action Agenda" that includes reducing methane, a greenhouse gas, and building climate-resilient cities, among other things. A central theme is electrification, with the aim of increasing the use of electricity — preferably from renewable energy such as solar and wind — from 21% to 35% by 2035, to reduce greenhouse emissions.During the negotiations, scheduled Nov. 9-20, delegates are also expected to take up the issue of helping poorer countries pay to adapt to rising temperatures and extreme weather events, both tied to climate change, and transition away from fossil fuels.The last two summits, COP30 in Brazil and COP29 in Azerbaijan, came under criticism for ending with little agreement on how to reduce greenhouse emissions. The final texts of those agreements didn't even mention fuels; at COP28 in Dubai, delegates agreed to transition away from fossil fuels.Undermining the summit, the United States, which is the world's second-largest polluter after China, will again be absent. During his first term, and again when he took office for a second time in January 2025, President Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. from climate negotiations."No single COP is a silver bullet that can stop climate change overnight," said U.N. Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell. "But every recent COP has made essential progress. COP31 in Antalya will, too."In a change from previous summits, COP31 is being jointly organized by Turkey and Australia after the two jostled over which would be the host. As a compromise, Turkey is the official host while Australia is leading the negotiations. news.title: Why Nvidia's board is investigating CEO Jensen Huang: All you need to know
news.text: US chipmaker Nvidia has launched an independent investigation following reports that its founder and Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation, the company's board of directors said in a statement on Sunday. The announcement follows reports by various publications that a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, allegedly developed a close relationship with Jensen Huang while gathering information for Beijing. The board, however, has said it has no reason to believe that US national security or Nvidia's confidential information was compromised. What exactly happened? The New York Times reported on Saturday that China's Ministry of State Security had recruited Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman, to gather intelligence on Jensen Huang. According to the report, a memo circulated among senior policymakers in the Trump administration last spring cited intelligence that Alice Huang was working for China's top intelligence agency. The alleged objective was to obtain information about Nvidia and its CEO, including potentially influencing the company to support making its most advanced AI chips available to China. Alice Huang was associated with Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed, which has been a significant Nvidia customer. The New York Times reported that Megaspeed had purchased more than $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the preceding two years. The reports also alleged that Jensen Huang had developed a close, personal relationship with Alice Huang. He subsequently acknowledged in a message to Nvidia's employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife and apologised to his family and colleagues. Why has Nvidia's board ordered an investigation? The board announced that it was initiating an independent investigation in light of the reporting. A committee of independent directors, assisted by external independent legal counsel, will oversee the inquiry. The board has made three points clear:It considers US national and economic security paramount to Nvidia and its shareholders.It has no reason to believe that national security or Nvidia's secrets were compromised.Huang supports the investigation and has committed to cooperating fully.The board has also reiterated its confidence in Huang and his leadership team. He is expected to continue leading Nvidia while the inquiry proceeds. Why Chinese connection particularly sensitive? The US government has imposed export restrictions to prevent China from accessing the most advanced American semiconductor technology. The restrictions are intended to limit China's ability to develop advanced AI and other strategic technologies with potential military applications. The New York Times reported that the alleged intelligence operation was intended not just to gather information but potentially to influence Nvidia's position on chip exports to China. Megaspeed's business relationship with Nvidia is also relevant because US authorities have reportedly scrutinised the company over suspicions that it helped Beijing obtain advanced chips restricted from export to China. The allegations have also gained political attention and three Republican committee chairs in the US House of Representatives asked Huang to brief Congress on his interactions with Alice Huang and Nvidia's safeguards for protecting sensitive information. They said the reports raised national security concerns about China's potential access to sensitive US technology and information. They sought a response by November 11. US President Donald Trump said on Sunday that he had not discussed the allegations with Huang, but described him as an honourable person and praised his contribution to Nvidia. ALSO READ: What Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said in email as board launches probe Why is Nvidia valuable? Nvidia sits at the centre of the US-China technology rivalry. Its advanced graphics processing units (GPUs) are essential for training and running sophisticated AI models. Its CUDA software platform allows developers to build and run applications on Nvidia GPUs. Thus, the company has become one of the most important suppliers of the infrastructure powering the global AI industry. Nvidia's latest reported quarterly results show that data centre operations accounted for the overwhelming bulk ($89 billion) of its quarterly revenue ($96.2 billion). For the full fiscal year 2026, Nvidia reported revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65 per cent from the previous year. Nvidia has become the world's second-most valuable publicly listed company after Apple, with a market capitalisation of approximately $4.5 trillion. But its stock has beein experiencing considerable volatility in recent weeks. As of November 6, Nvidia shares closed at approximately $186.64. The stock had fallen for five consecutive weeks and was around 22 per cent below its October 6 record closing level. The decline had wiped out approximately $1.27 trillion in market value from its peak. ALSO READ: Nvidia CEO Huang admits affair with Chinese spy, company launches probe The investigation introduces another source of uncertainty for a stock already facing pressure from concerns about the sustainability of AI spending. Reuters quoted Dan Ives of Yorkville Ives & Co as saying that the investigation could create risks for the stock because of Huang's importance to Nvidia's global strategy. However, the market reaction is yet to be seen as the board's announcement came after the US market had closed on Friday.
news.summary: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang will remain in his role as the company's board investigates reports that he was targeted by a foreign intelligence operation

news.title: Rubio says Trump's war against Iran not 'necessarily popular' but needed to stop a nuclear threat
news.text: HOMESTEAD AIR RESERVE BASE — Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that President Donald Trump launched the war against Iran even if it was not 'necessarily popular' to safeguard the world from the country's nuclear ambitions.He would not comment directly about the Republican wipeout in Tuesday's elections, which delivered a resounding rebuke to Trump. The unpopularity of the Iran war and its impact on gasoline prices and other parts of the economy helped Democrats seize control of Congress.Asked about Vice President JD Vance's social media post last week that largely blamed the war for the Republican losses, Rubio told reporters that Trump 'identified a very real threat' in Iran and worked to stop the Islamic Republic from pursuing a nuclear weapon.'He addressed it even though oftentimes the right thing to do for the country — confronting difficult challenges for the security of our country — doing it isn't necessarily popular, but necessary,' Rubio said in Florida before heading to a Group of 7 foreign ministers meeting in Paris.America's top diplomat offered a robust defense of the more than eight-month-old war even as voters blamed Trump's policies for the hit to their pocketbooks, including higher energy prices that stemmed from disruptions to shipments in the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway where one-fifth of the world's oil transited before the war.Rubio and Vance offer differing comments on the warRubio's comments also put him at odds with Vance, who are both considered possible 2028 contenders. Asked in a '60 Minutes' interview that aired Sunday about potential candidates other than Vance, Trump named Rubio, saying that 'I think Marco's great' but noting there was a 'tremendous bench' in his Republican Party and that 'maybe I'm better off not getting involved.'Trump told reporters Sunday that Vance was right about the war's impact on the election — other than that his vice president should have also insisted it was the correct choice to go to war.'I can tell you if I had it to do again, this historically — for history — will go down as one of the best things we ever did,' Trump said. 'Because if they ever had a nuclear weapon, they would blow up the world.'Iran has long maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran has 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90%.Asked on '60 Minutes' whether he would escalate the war following the elections, Trump said, 'Well I'm not looking to. I don't think there's any reason to.'Rubio says Iran talks aren't on the 'verge of a breakthrough'With no clear administration strategy to wind down the conflict and the Middle East on edge over the possibility of a return to major hostilities, mediators are trying to revive talks between the sides.Rubio said, 'I wouldn't say we're at the verge of a breakthrough.'He reiterated that Trump prefers a diplomatic solution, but 'right now, it hasn't been very productive because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable, but in some cases outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.'Trump is set to meet Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House on Monday, according to his official schedule.The Associated Press has reported that Iran was reviewing proposals presented by chief mediator Qatar aimed at addressing differences with the United States about Tehran's nuclear program. But Iran was seen as unwilling to negotiate with the Trump administration over their atomic activities until the U.S. agrees to several core conditions that Tehran has been demanding be part of any ceasefire agreement, officials have said.Those include ending the U.S. blockade on Iran's ports, lifting sanctions, unfreezing its assets, issuing compensation for war damage and ending hostilities throughout the region, including Israeli operations in Lebanon.While Rubio said there was no diplomatic breakthrough at hand, Trump told CNN in a phone interview Sunday that as long as the U.S. sees progress in negotiations with Tehran and they sign a 'strong agreement,' it's 'highly unlikely it's going to be necessary' to resume strikes.Trump said, however, that the U.S. had identified infrastructure targets, including 38 bridges, that it would strike if military action resumes.The U.S. military, meanwhile, still has carried out limited strikes on Iran, including against its air defenses, at least twice over the past week. It also fired on and disabled a commercial ship Saturday that the U.S. says was trying to breach its naval blockade on Iranian ports.Rubio acknowledged that the U.S. will take defensive actions if needed.'If there's a clear and present threat to shipping or to our forces in the region, we have a right to defend ourselves,' Rubio said.

news.title: Trump vows comeback as bitter showdown with Congress looms
news.text: WASHINGTON, United States — Donald Trump vowed a political comeback Sunday as the major parties clashed over Democrat threats to prosecute top administration officials after the president's Republicans lost control of Congress in midterm elections.The devastating results in last Tuesday's vote leave Trump politically hamstrung as he enters the remaining two-year 'lame duck' period of his White House tenure. It also opens the door to multiple investigations by the Democrat-controlled Congress of the president, his family and senior members of his administration.On political talk shows Sunday, incoming congressional leaders from the Democratic Party promised to hold Trump and his aides to account, while the president's top law officer resolved to defend them and Trump dug in his heels on social media.'America took a giant step back in History with the results of the last Election,' Trump said in a post on Truth Social, adding that the stock market that had grown during his tenure took a loss after the vote.'But have no fear, we will be back, BIGGER AND STRONGER THAN EVER BEFORE!'On Friday, a defiant Trump appointed hardline advisor Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, signaling a bare-knuckle fightback -- even though many Republicans, including Vice President JD Vance, have reflected on why they had lost so badly at the ballot box.Miller was architect of Trump's tough immigration policy, which analysts have identified as a contributing factor to the unpopularity of Republicans and their election debacle.Amid Democrat threats for administration officials to 'lawyer up,' Trump said Saturday he was ordering the Justice Department to examine Democratic threats to impeach members of his administration, likening it to 'extortion.'Impeaching Hegseth? With control of committees in both chambers of Congress, Democrats can summon officials, demand documents and hold public hearings, putting Trump and his senior aides under intense scrutiny.Likely subjects include the Trump family's business and cryptocurrency dealings, government contracts involving billionaire Elon Musk, cuts to federal agencies, immigration enforcement and the conduct of the Iran war.Hakeem Jeffries, set to become speaker of the new Democrat-controlled House of Representatives, said he would support an effort to oust Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, a key architect of the war on Iran that began in February.'I'm a hard yes on the Hegseth resolution,' Jeffries told ABC, when asked about a Republican lawmaker's reported plan to introduce an impeachment motion as early as Monday.'The so-called secretary of defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.'Trump on Sunday defended Hegseth when talking with reporters, saying: 'I mean he's guilty of two things, basically winning two wars,' referring to the US raid on Venezuela in January that removed president Nicholas Maduro and the ongoing war with Iran.'We won in Venezuela. We've taken out hundreds of billions of dollars. We won in 48 minutes. And we won in Iran,' Trump told reporters. 'It's just a question of closing it out now or later.'Attorney General Todd Blanche, a former personal lawyer for Trump and now head of the Justice Department, vowed to actively defend Trump and senior members of his administration.'If they try to come after Stephen Miller...instead of actually just conducting oversight and leading, of course the Department of Justice will be there to defend him,' Blanche told CNN.Robert Garcia, the ranking Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, took aim at Blanche, saying one role of Congress under the US constitution is to hold the executive branch to account.'All he wants to do is protect Donald Trump, is protect Donald Trump's cabinet and administration officials. That is not his job,' Garcia told CNN, vowing to stop corruption and investigate 'those that are committing crimes against the American public.''They can come after us however they want. We're not going to be intimidated,' added Garcia.

news.title: Trump reacts to the Jensen Huang affair: 'He probably has an excuse for it'
news.text: President Donald Trump backed Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang on Sunday after Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife with a woman US intelligence reportedly suspects was a Chinese spy. news.title: After midterm rout, Vance tries to build his own 2028 brand
news.text:
Late in his blitz to salvage Republicans' midterm fortunes, Vice President JD Vance shifted strategy. He talked less about President Donald Trump and more about the issues that define his own political identity.

Vance argued the case ​for Republicans, who lost control of Congress in Tuesday’s vote, almost exclusively through the lens of his policy portfolio, according to a Reuters review of half a dozen speeches since the ‌Republican convention in September.

He bypassed Trump's signature policies, including the Iran war and deportations, as polls showed the president's sagging popularity dragging down Republican office-seekers.

The change was deliberate, according to two people familiar with the strategy. Vance and his advisers saw the issues he championed — economic nationalism, foreign policy restraint, and public safety — as politically potent subjects he could address with authority. While Trump embraced them as part of his MAGA movement, people said Vance had emerged as their lead crusader.

The shift offered an early glimpse of ​how the 42-year-old vice president could chart his own course as Republicans begin looking beyond Trump.

Vance hasn’t said whether he will run for president in 2028, and Trump hasn’t endorsed him or anyone else. ​But Vance is viewed as a leading potential contender who some Republican officials say will need to inherit much of Trump’s coalition while separating himself from his boss's ⁠baggage.

Vance took a more public step on Wednesday toward reinforcing his own political brand with an unusually blunt election postmortem. In a social media post, he blamed the Iran war for Republicans’ midterm defeat and laid out a ​platform for a Republican rebound.

He called for a swift end to the conflict and urged Republicans to focus on affordability, reevaluate foreign relations and overhaul the US relationship with Israel.

Trump has called Americans’ affordability concerns a Democratic “hoax.” He ​launched a war against Iran following sustained lobbying from Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Trump went on to endorse Netanyahu in the Israeli election.

VANCE MAKES UNEASE AT THE WAR PUBLIC

The post for the first time put Vance openly on the side of ending the war.

Three people familiar with the White House and Vance's communications told Reuters that the vice president was not breaking with Trump and said White House chief of staff Susie Wiles knew in advance about Vance's post.

On Friday, Trump reshuffled senior White House leadership, replacing ​Wiles with Stephen Miller in a move that suggests the White House plans to double down on some of Trump’s more hardline policies.

Trump has acknowledged the Iran war played a role in the Republican rout because of the ​resulting high gas prices but has continued to defend it. "I would have done nothing different," he told reporters on Wednesday.

Reuters could not determine whether Trump knew about the post in advance.

Donald Trump Jr., the president's eldest son, endorsed Vance's remarks ‌on social media, ⁠along with some conservative allies.

The dialogue further elevated Vance as a potential post-Trump conservative standard-bearer, said Michael Ricci, a Republican strategist and former adviser to House Speakers John Boehner and Paul Ryan.

USING THE MEGAPHONE OF THE VICE PRESIDENCY

He said Vance’s message forced conservatives to debate the merits of the war, and more broadly, what core tenets Republican presidential candidates should embrace in 2028.

"It’s simplistic to say this about him looking for ways to differentiate himself from Trump," Ricci said. "This is about him using his megaphone of the vice presidency to set the terms of debate."

Representatives for Vance declined to comment. White House representatives referred Reuters to Trump's comments on Wednesday, when he told reporters he understood ​Vance's perspective on the election results.

Democrats are poised to ​tie Vance – or any Republican nominee – to Trump ⁠in 2028, especially if Trump plays a large role in vetting conservative hopefuls.

"There’s a real challenge of how you position yourself to be viable in a general election while winning a primary that still requires you to bow down and kiss the ring,” said Igor Volsky, a Democratic strategist.

Vance’s brand did not emerge from the midterms unscathed. ​Republicans lost in states where he campaigned. Some of the strategies he endorsed – including an ad by Ohio gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy that cast doubt on the ​sexual abuse suffered by the ⁠victorious Democratic candidate, Amy Acton – may have swung races away from Republicans.

Other possible 2028 presidential contenders have offered their diagnoses of the midterm defeat. Texas Senator Ted Cruz said Republicans hadn't done enough on affordability. 

Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said losing candidates had focused too heavily on transgender issues and neglected voter concerns about data centres and artificial intelligence. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has stayed silent.

Vance's effort to shape the debate was visible in the campaign's closing days.

In stump ​speeches, he told voters to support Republicans because they would investigate fraud in federal health care and antipoverty programs, tying that to the ​White House's immigration agenda and cost of living. He almost entirely ignored the Iran war and gas prices, and seldom mentioned Trump by name.

“I want my kids to raise a family in a country that is vibrant and thriving and free and prosperous. I want the ​simple things,” Vance told one of his final rallies in North Carolina. “And because I want that for me, I want it for you too.”
news.summary: Late in his blitz to salvage Republicans' midterm fortunes, Vice President JD Vance shifted strategy. He talked less about President Donald Trump and more about the issues that define his own political identity.

news.title: Rubio defends Trump's decision to go to war with Iran as US president prepares to meet Qatar's PM
news.text: Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Sunday that President Donald Trump launched the war against Iran even if it was not “necessarily popular” to safeguard the world from the country's nuclear ambitions. His statement comes as Trump plans to meet Qatar's prime minister on Monday as the key mediator pushes new proposals in talks with Iran. Rubio would not comment directly about the Republican wipeout in Tuesday’s elections, which delivered a resounding rebuke to Trump. The unpopularity of the Iran war and its impact on gasoline prices and other parts of the economy helped Democrats seize control of Congress. Asked about Vice President JD Vance’s social media post last week that largely blamed the war for the Republican losses, Rubio told reporters that Trump “identified a very real threat” in Iran and worked to stop the Islamic Republic from pursuing a nuclear weapon. “He addressed it even though oftentimes the right thing to do for the country — confronting difficult challenges for the security of our country — doing it isn’t necessarily popular, but necessary,” Rubio said in Florida before heading to a Group of 7 foreign ministers meeting in Paris. America's top diplomat offered a robust defense of the more than eight-month-old war even as voters blamed Trump’s policies for the hit to their pocketbooks, including higher energy prices that stemmed from disruptions to shipments in the Strait of Hormuz, a crucial waterway where one-fifth of the world's oil transited before the war. Rubio's comments also put him at odds with Vance amid speculation of both of their 2028 presidential ambitions. Trump told reporters Sunday that Vance was right — other than that his vice president should have also insisted it was the correct choice to go to war. “I can tell you if I had it to do again, this historically — for history — will go down as one of the best things we ever did," Trump said. "Because if they ever had a nuclear weapon, they would blow up the world." ran has long maintained that its nuclear program is peaceful. According to the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran has 440.9 kilograms (972 pounds) of uranium that is enriched up to 60% purity, a short, technical step from weapons-grade levels of 90%. With no clear administration strategy to wind down the conflict and the Middle East on edge over the possibility of a return to major hostilities, mediators are trying to revive talks between the sides. Rubio said, “I wouldn’t say we’re at the verge of a breakthrough.” He reiterated that Trump prefers a diplomatic solution, but “right now, it hasn’t been very productive because the Iranian demands are simply not just unacceptable, but in some cases outrageous and ridiculous and really not realistic.” Trump is set to meet Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani at the White House on Monday, according to his official schedule. The Associated Press has reported that Iran was reviewing proposals presented by chief mediator Qatar aimed at addressing differences with the United States about Tehran’s nuclear program. But Iran was seen as unwilling to negotiate with the Trump administration over their atomic activities until the U.S. agrees to several core conditions that Tehran has been demanding be part of any ceasefire agreement, officials have said. Those include ending the U.S. blockade on Iran’s ports, lifting sanctions, unfreezing its assets, issuing compensation for war damage and ending hostilities throughout the region, including Israeli operations in Lebanon. While Rubio said there was no diplomatic breakthrough at hand, Trump told CNN in a phone interview Sunday that as long as the U.S. sees progress in negotiations with Tehran and they sign a “strong agreement,” it’s “highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary” to resume strikes. Trump said, however, that the U.S. had identified infrastructure targets, including 38 bridges, that it would strike if military action resumes. The U.S. military, meanwhile, still has carried out limited strikes on Iran, including against its air defenses, at least twice over the past week. It also fired on and disabled a commercial ship Saturday that the U.S. says was trying to breach its naval blockade on Iranian ports. Rubio acknowledged that the U.S. will take defensive actions if needed. “If there’s a clear and present threat to shipping or to our forces in the region, we have a right to defend ourselves,” Rubio said.
news.summary: Qatar is the key mediator in talks with Iran which is reviewing proposals aimed at addressing differences with the United States about Tehran’s nuclear program; Rubio told reporters that Trump “identified a very real threat” in Iran and worked to stop it from pursuing a nuclear weapon
