news.title: 'Nerve-wracking' wait in Mississippi for US Senate vote result
news.text: JACKSON: Mississippi residents faced a "nerve-wracking" wait to see whether the southern state elects its first Black senator in more than a century as vote-counting dragged on Sunday after this past week's US midterms.Voters who spoke to AFP in the state capital Jackson on Saturday anticipated that history could be in the making in the whisker-close race between Democrat Scott Colom, an African-American man, and Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, a white woman.With 97 percent of the vote counted by Sunday afternoon, Colom was 2,574 votes ahead of Hyde-Smith -- a gap of just 0.3 percentage points.Mississippi has not elected a Democratic senator since 1982, and Colom would be its first Black senator in nearly 150 years -- since the Reconstruction era following the American Civil War that ended slavery.Gregory Glass, a 47-year-old restaurant owner, himself an African-American, said a victory for Colom would be "historic" but admitted to having "bittersweet" feelings about that."It should have happened sooner than that, especially in Mississippi, in a state that has so many African-Americans in it," said Glass.According to the US Census Bureau, more than one-third of the state's population, long viewed as a bastion of Republican politics, is Black.A victory for Colom would also put another staunchly Republican state -- including Texas, South Carolina and Kansas -- in the Democrats' column for Senate in Tuesday's election.The midterms were a resounding win for Democrats, who seized control of both houses of Congress as voters nationwide delivered a stinging rebuke to Republican President Donald Trump.- 'Every single vote' -But the count is not over yet..Trump says offer of press secretary role to UFC chief was a joke.The unusually long wait reflects Mississippi's election procedures, which allow officials several days to process mail-in and provisional ballots -- potentially enough to decide the contest.Jermal Clark, election commissioner for Hinds County, which includes the city of Jackson, said that they were still going through so-called "affidavit" provisional ballots.These are cast by people whose eligibility cannot be confirmed at polling stations, sometimes because of missing identification or discrepancies in voter registration records."We're in the process of counting them for the accuracy and the checking to see if each individual lives in the precinct that they say they live in," Clark told AFP.Secretary of State Michael Watson posted on X on Friday that 11,202 affidavit ballots have now been processed with roughly 78 percent of them being accepted.He also said there are also just under 2,900 outstanding absentee ballots."I'm just amazed at how so many communities and these election people are coming together to make sure every single vote is cast," said voter Coretta Fraser, a human resources manager..Indian Americans voted against Trump over domestic woes as bilateral ties took backseat.- 'We're excited' -"We're excited. You know, it's good to be part of something historic," said bakery manager Ebony Jones, who viewed Colom's potential win as a relief from years of bad news like the COVID pandemic and the development of artificial intelligence.The close contest has prompted both parties to deploy lawyers, with Republicans demanding that officials preserve records relating to the outstanding ballots in anticipation of possible legal challenges.Mississippi has no automatic recount procedure, although candidates can seek court intervention.For Glass, the restaurant owner, the voters' verdict can't come soon enough."The waiting is a little bit nerve-wracking because you want them to just call it," he said, making clear his preference for Colom to win."And I'm sure people on the other side of it don't necessarily want that," he said. news.title: Trump Offers Bizarre Excuse After Favorite Tech Lord Admits to Affair
news.text:
Donald Trump has responded with a bizarre word salad after being asked about billionaire Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s extramarital affair with a suspected Chinese spy. 

On Sunday, Nvidia opened an investigation into Huang after he informed the company’s board about his intimate relationship with Alice Huang, a business executive whom U.S. intelligence determined was a top spy for Beijing, according to reporting from the New York Times. 

Huang has been one of Trump’s closest allies in Silicon Valley. 

Speaking to reporters during a gaggle in West Palm Beach, Trump was asked whether the revelation had changed his mind about taking Huang on his upcoming trip to Asia, where he and Chinese President Xi Jinping are expected to discuss the ongoing AI race. 

Trump will land in Manila, Philippines, on Nov. 15 and end his trip in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19. Huang has not been confirmed to be among the president’s guests. 

“I’d certainly take him,” Trump responded. “I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong. He dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else.”

When another reporter informed him of Nvidia’s investigation into Huang, Trump seemed to stand by his old tech buddy, 

“He’s a fine person, in my opinion,” he said. “I think he’s an honorable guy, I think he probably has an excuse for it… He’s done an amazing job for our country.” 

In an earlier statement to the Daily Beast, Huang said, “I was unfaithful to my wife… My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting NVIDIA and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.”

Trump said Sunday night that he did not regret a lack of action on his part. According to the New York Times, officials told Trump in May that Alice-who had connections to major U.S. chip producers and the Chinese government-was conducting foreign surveillance on Huang. 

Despite these warnings, Trump had Huang accompany him on his trip to China later that month. 

American officials told the New York Times that they suspected Huang’s mistress was assisting China in their efforts to gain access to advanced AI chips, but that Trump chose not to act on the information at the time. A memo determined that she was purchasing chips and smuggling them into China. 

Huang long advocated for selling AI chips to China, arguing in the past that Nvidia having a stake in Chinese chip sales would benefit the U.S. market.

news.title: Trump makes Dana White U-turn as he announces Iran War close to end and Russia-China meeting on cards
news.text: Donald Trump has performed a dramatic U-turn by claiming he was “only kidding” about hiring UFC president Dana White as the White House Press Secretary. The President made his comments in a wide-ranging interview where he also revealed he is organising “de-nuclearisation” talks with Russia and China next week. Trump also addressed his relationship with Vice-President JD Vance, who said the Iran War was to blame for the Republicans’ disastrous midterm election results . Trump rebuked Vance, saying “a lot of people did not like his comments”. Trump’s interview , held on the tarmac before he jetted off from the airport near Mar-A-Lago that bears his name in West Palm Beach, was also notable for his attire. The President was not wearing his usual bright red ‘Make America Great Again’ baseball cap. Instead, he is sporting cream and gold headwear with USA emblazoned front and centre. A gold US flag was visible on the side. It appears to be similar to other hats Trump has worn in his second Presidency, but some have noted the fact he did not promote the MAGA brand in the wake of the Republicans’ heavy midterm election losses. The interview was one of his first since the devastating defeat — and this is what Trump said. Following the midterms, Trump has reorganised his top team, bringing in ICE supremo Stephen Miller as his new White House chief of staff. Trump still needs to fill the vacant press secretary job since Katie Zacharia’s an ill-fated stint in the role last month. She quit after only five days in the job, holding just one short press conference, making Zacharia’s tenure the shortest in history. Trump identified his chosen candidate over the weekend — UFC President Dana White. In a post on Truth Social, the US President said: “I am pleased to announce that the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior, has been offered the job of Press Secretary of the United States.” However, in Sunday evening’s interview, Trump said he wasn’t serious about the appointment. He added: “I will tell you I was only kidding but Dana loves the idea. There’s only one Dana. He is great. “You would not mess around with him so much. I was kidding of course, when you look at the fighters I put on I said some do not come from our country, they come from parts unknown. I was kidding but I think Dana likes the idea.” In his original social media statement, Trump suggested White could be helped by several UFC fighters to “defend us against the lunatic left” before adding “Dana, please take the job!” Figures on the right of the Republican party — often called MAGA — have said a reshuffle will not do enough to win voters back in 2028’s Presidential election after the Democrats claimed several stunning wins in very traditionally conservative areas, including southern states like Texas and Georgia. Those victories mean the Democrats now control both houses of Congress, and several high-profile governorships. MAGA has hit out at Trump’s decision to launch military action in Iran after he pledged ‘no more wars’ in the 2024 campaign. They include Vice-President JD Vance, who said "the reason we lost is the war". While Trump has accepted the war is partly to blame for his party’s electoral catastrophe, he appeared to hit back at Vance’s claim. He told reporters: “A lot of people did not like his comments. He should have made one other statement which I think is very important — ‘if you had to do it again, the answer is yes’. “I can tell you if you had to do it again, for history will go down as one of the biggest things we ever did. If they ever had a nuclear weapon they would blow up the world . You know why? Because they are crazy.” The President insisted his relationship with Vance has not been affected by the difference in opinion. However Trump appears to have heard the message from voters, telling reporters the US is close to ending the war in Iran soon. The conflict is unpopular in America as it has driven up the cost of living. He claimed American forces “are doing well” and said the end is in sight due to blockades on Iranian imports. He said: “We are choking it off. We have Operation Iron Gate just went into effect. That means nothing comes in by land and as you know with the naval blockade nothing comes in by water so we have it very well blocked off.” International relations have dominated Trump’s second term, and looks like it will continue to do so as the President also said he will have a three-way meeting with Russia and China next week. He added: “I am going to be going to China next week. One of the meetings will be with President Putin and President Xi and that will be interesting. We will talk about a lot of things, including de-nuclearisation.” He has previously talked up similar moves, but China rejected the offer only last month, claiming “it is neither fair, reasonable nor realistic to ask China to join the so-called trilateral nuclear disarmament negotiations at this stage”.
news.summary: The President has given one of his first interviews since the Republicans' devastating midterms losses, talking Iran, Dana White, JD Vance, and a Russia-China meeting

Huang engaged in an affair with Alice Huang, an AI executive whose Singapore-based data center company, Megaspeed, had become one of Nvidia’s biggest customers in Southeast Asia, the New York Times reported. Megaspeed bought more than $4.8 billion in chips since June 2024, according to the outlet. 

A highly classified spring 2025 memo warned top Trump administration policymakers that Ms. Huang had been recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to learn more about U.S.-made AI chips and possibly influence Nvidia to push for the most advanced of such chips to be made in China, according to the Times. American authorities reportedly suspected that Ms. Huang had been smuggling such chips to China.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio oversaw the drafting of the memo, the outlet separately reported.

Both Huangs are no relation, according to the outlet.

Huang, an influential ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, had advocated selling all but the most advanced chips to China. (RELATED: Nvidia CEO Praises China’s ‘Excellent’ Models As Free AI Boosts Hardware Sales)

Trump told reporters Sunday that he would “certainly take” Huang with him on an upcoming trip to China, according to the Times. 

“I mean, we’d have to find — I haven’t heard he’s done anything wrong,” Mr. Trump said. “He dealt with somebody, but you know, so does everybody else,” Trump reportedly added.

news.title: Democrats Plan to Push Clean Energy to Lower Bills and Challenge Trump’s Fossil Fuel Agenda
news.text:
Some Democrats are promising to push for more clean energy to help tackle rising energy costs when they take control of Congress in January, though President Donald Trump says he will use his veto power aggressively.

With new majorities in the House and Senate after last week’s midterms, Democrats can set an agenda boosting clean energy and addressing climate change. While those are traditionally core priorities of the party, climate was not a central topic in this election cycle.

Democrats can begin investigations and hold hearings into climate policy rollbacks and elimination of green energy grants by the Republican administration, potentially trying to undo some changes and restore renewable energy incentives.

Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island, the top Democrat on the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works, said Trump’s clean energy attacks drove up prices for taxpayers. He said Democrats will “work every angle to lower consumers’ energy costs, and we will demand accountability for the massive corruption wrought by Trump’s fossil-fuel donors.”

American Clean Power Association CEO Jason Grumet said everybody who is trying to build clean energy “feels bolstered.”

Enacting major changes would require Republican support because Democrats will lack the numbers to override presidential vetoes. Even then, lower energy bills are not guaranteed because prices also depend on fuel costs, demand and the expense of maintaining the electric grid.

“The wins give Democrats more leverage over spending and more political power to advance a coherent agenda; the question is whether they’ll use that power effectively,” said Lisa Sachs, director of the Columbia Center on Sustainable Investment. “The vote was for affordability and opportunity. Democrats now need to be clear about which policies deliver them.”

Trump holds veto power but thinks he and Democrats can deal

Trump said after Tuesday’s election that Democrats will send over “things that are insane” and he will veto them, speaking generally about legislation. But in the comments to Fox News, he predicted that “after a couple of months of vetoes,” he and Democrats will find ways to work together.

The White House said in a statement Wednesday that Trump is “committed to unleashing reliable, affordable, and secure energy sources to lower prices, strengthen our grid, and protect our national security, and is willing to work with anyone to accomplish this.”

Trump promised to lower energy prices. Instead, his war with Iran and other policies increased the price of gasoline, diesel and electricity. At the same time, the administration canceled many clean energy projects and grants and slowed clean energy permitting.

Trump particularly dislikes offshore wind. Developer Orsted said Thursday that Revolution Wind, a large wind farm in federal waters off Rhode Island, has started operating commercially.

Will the president change his tune on green energy? That’s doubtful, said former Sen. Byron Dorgan, D-N.D., co-chair of the government relations practice at ArentFox Schiff.

“He is likely to keep pushing his energy issues, and I think he will be forced to give some room for a new Congress to recreate a different strategy that will add clean energy,” Dorgan said in an email.

Trump promotes expanding production of oil, natural gas and coal, which cause climate change, because he argues that would give the U.S. the lowest-cost electricity. Mike Sommers, CEO of the American Petroleum Institute, the oil and gas industry’s top lobbying group, said that as voters have changed the balance of political power in Washington, “the affordability message is unmistakable.”

Sommers said in a statement there is a real opportunity for bipartisan cooperation to reduce costs and strengthen the economy, starting with an energy permitting reform proposal announced in September. The Senate is expected to hold a procedural vote Monday on the legislation, which is aimed at shortening the timeline to get big energy projects started.

Ife Kilimanjaro, executive director of the U.S. Climate Action Network, said Democrats should reject that proposal and use their stronger position to pass legislation that actually builds out much-needed clean energy.

Reversing Trump’s anti-climate policies

The administration has reshaped the Environmental Protection Agency, reversing pollution limits as it promotes fossil fuels.

Clear Street energy transition analyst Tim Moore said he expects Democrats to investigate the climate and environmental rollbacks, in an effort to block some from taking effect. Democrats could also try amending the Clean Air Act to cut carbon pollution and push back against EPA budget cuts, he added.

Rep. Sean Casten, D-Ill., said he is cautiously optimistic some Republicans will now seek to differentiate themselves from Trump and back pro-environmental policies. But without Republican support, Democrats’ more ambitious bills will largely lay out their agenda for 2028, he added.

Climate is not necessarily at the top of Democrats’ list of priorities. They are targeting healthcare access, trade tariffs and the Iran war.

Rep. Frank Pallone, the New Jersey Democrat who is expected to become chair of the House Energy and Commerce Committee, said the party should focus on healthcare, affordability, consumer and environmental protections, clean energy and regulating Big Tech.

A potential stalemate seen on clean energy and climate policy

David Victor, a professor of innovation and public policy at the University of California, San Diego, largely expects a stalemate at the federal level on climate and energy policy because of the divided government. He said agreement could come on some bipartisan measures such as a permitting overhaul.

Victor thinks Democratic-led investigations and hearings will center on corruption and other topics that may only touch on energy and climate. Like Casten, Victor said many of the Democratic bills likely will not become law, but will outline what Democrats could accomplish if they win the White House in 2028.

“The Democrats are going to be drafting things that the administration’s not going to like. They don’t have the votes to override a veto, and on top of it, the administration is going to be in turmoil because of its own electoral failures and because of all the investigations,” Victor said. “This seems to me, at the federal level, largely a recipe for kind of intense chaos over the next two years.”

One of the biggest wild cards is the behavior of the administration, which could use executive power to double down on rollbacks of climate and environmental rules, he said.

States could advance clean energy without waiting for Congress

Democrats scored victories in races for governor in states long controlled by Republicans, including Texas and Georgia.

Leah Stokes, a political scientist at the UC Santa Barbara, said there could be a lot of state action on climate next year because of those wins. That is where climate leadership has traditionally come from, she noted. At the federal level, Stokes is optimistic about extending clean energy tax credits since some Republicans support that.

Jay Inslee, a former Democratic governor and congressman from Washington, also expects growing momentum for clean energy in states that elected Democratic governors, particularly in states where they also won legislative majorities.

“This is a really powerful instrument for the United States to join the rest of the world and get back in a leadership position, even if we still have a climate denier that might exercise a veto on some things that we want to do federally,” Inslee said. “So I hope people will pay attention to the big progress we’re going to make on a state-level basis.”
news.summary:
Some Democrats are promising to push for more clean energy to help tackle rising energy costs when they take control of Congress in January, though President Donald Trump says he will use his veto power aggressively. With new majorities in the House and Senate after last week's midterms, Democrats can set an agenda boosting clean energy and addressing climate change. While those are traditionally core priorities of the party, climate was not a central topic in this election cycle. Democrats can begin investigations and hold hearings into climate policy rollbacks and elimination of green energy grants by the Republican administration, potentially trying to undo some changes and restore renewable energy incentives.

news.title: G7 Ministers Meet on Efforts to End Ukraine Conflict, Halt New Iran War
news.text: PARIS: Foreign ministers of the G7 group meet in Paris from Monday for two days of talks expected to see European powers press the United States to seek a fair settlement for Ukraine in the war against Russia and deter Washington from further military action against Iran. Ministers from the leading industrialised nations of Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States will be gathering with preoccupations strikingly similar to those of the last such meeting in March. Russia's war against Ukraine following the February 2022 full-scale invasion of its neighbour is grinding towards its fifth anniversary. And Washington is still not ruling out new attacks against Iran even after the defeat of President Donald Trump's Republicans in the midterms. All eyes will be on US Secretary of State Marco Rubio who is due to attend both days, unlike the March meeting where he only came for one. This G7 ministerial meeting, one of the final acts of the French G7 presidency that saw President Emmanuel Macron host Donald Trump for the leaders' summit this summer in the lakeside resort of Evian, had long been scheduled to be held in the southern port city of Marseille. But at the last minute the event was moved to Paris, with only scheduling reasons given for the change. The visit by Rubio -- seen by US media as a potential candidate to succeed Trump -- will be his first abroad since the midterms. Washington will also in 2027 take over the G7 presidency from France. - 'Europeans will be represented' - The meeting coincides with US-mediated talks with Moscow and Kyiv in Abu Dhabi scheduled for Tuesday and Wednesday on ending the Ukraine war, with Europe concerned Kyiv must not be forced to accept disadvantageous conditions. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot told RTL radio that on this occasion "Europeans will be represented and France will be in Abu Dhabi to participate in these talks". Trump stoked fears of a US pivot toward the Kremlin by predicting a "very big" deal with Russia involving not only the Ukraine war but "all of Europe". Jared Kushner, the US president's envoy and son-in-law, said the United States was working on "a broader European security architecture that can help establish the conditions for lasting peace", a concept met with scepticism in the past by Europe. On Iran, Trump has not ruled out new strikes, including at so-called Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected nuclear site which Tehran denies is such a facility. Europeans, however, are eager to see a resolution and shipping traffic return to normal in the Strait of Hormuz energy transit hub. "We're dealing with them now," Trump said of the Iranians Friday. "They want to make a deal very badly." The sidelines of the meeting will also see the French finance ministry hosting on Monday a donor conference to raise funds to repair the dome protecting the nuclear reactor that exploded in Ukraine's Chernobyl in 1986 after it was damaged in a Russian strike last year. Around 500 million euros is required but only just over half has been raised so far with a target date of spring 2027 to muster the rest of the funds, the French finance ministry told AFP. Even though the meeting was moved to Paris, Marseille will still host the launch of a network of 14 global ports uniting to combat drug trafficking, which has become a major scourge in the southern city, Barrot said. As he addressed reporters while preparing to leave for France, Rubio declined to comment directly on Trump's and the Republicans' crushing loss in the US midterm elections. "It is not uncommon to have a division of power in this country," Rubio told reporters, alluding to the fact that Trump will now see both houses of Congress controlled by the Democrats. Asked about widespread protests in France, Rubio added that he was not worried and trusted US counterparts on the ground who advised him it is safe to attend the G7 meeting.
news.summary: All eyes will be on US Secretary of State Marco Rubio who is due to attend both days

news.title: Trump to meet Qatar’s prime minister as Iran diplomacy faces hurdles
news.text:
President Donald Trump will meet with Qatar's prime minister at the White House on Monday, ​according to the White House schedule, as the ‌conflict with Iran drags on and diplomatic efforts to end it face significant obstacles.

Trump is due to meet with Sheikh ​Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, who also serves as ​Qatar's foreign minister, in a closed-door meeting. ⁠Vice President JD Vance is also scheduled to ​meet with the Qatari leader, according to a US ​official.

Qatar has played a central role as an intermediary between Washington and Tehran, conveying proposals and seeking to bridge ​differences over Iran's nuclear program and the terms ​for ending the conflict.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Sunday ‌that ⁠negotiations with Iran had made little progress and that he did not see an imminent breakthrough. 

Speaking before departing Florida for a G7 foreign ministers meeting ​in Paris, ​Rubio said ⁠Trump preferred a diplomatic solution but described Iran's demands as "unacceptable" and, in some ​cases, "outrageous and ridiculous, and really not ​realistic."

Trump said ⁠Sunday that he was highly unlikely to order new strikes against Iran if negotiations made progress and produced a ⁠strong ​agreement, but warned that the ​United States had identified additional infrastructure targets, including bridges, should military ​action resume.

news.title: Trump says his deportation policy 'might have been too tough' for voters
news.text: President Donald Trump in his first major interview since his party lost control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections said he thinks his administration was too aggressive on deportations and that he thinks he can work with Democrats in the new Congress on some kind of immigration deal.Trump said his deportation policy was part of the reason Republicans lost, telling CBS's "60 Minutes" in an interview that aired on Sunday: "I think it might be too tough, yeah." He added that he thinks he could reach an agreement with the new Democratic majority. "The deal would be we would work something out. And I think it's something -- I think that's something that's actually doable," he said in the interview.Trump did not give specifics about what that deal would look like - and shortly after taping the interview on Friday, Trump named the key architect of his hard-line immigration agenda, Stephen Miller, as his new chief of staff."Trump says his immigration crackdown went too far," Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer scoffed on social media Sunday after the interview aired. "Apparently, his solution was to put the man responsible for it in charge of the White House. That's not a course correction. That's a promotion." The president's immigration crackdown was a prominent feature of his return to office with major operations in multiple cities sending arrests soaring. Two US citizens - Renee Good and Alex Pretti - were killed by federal officers during protests against the operations.Democrats have said oversight of Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security is a priority for the new Congress.Trump said he believes that "killers" and "drug dealers" in the country illegally should be deported, but suggested he was open to the idea of a deal that would let others stay "if they're good people working in a landscaping company, or working in a hotel, or doing something, right? And in some cases, paying taxes.

news.text: Hong Kong: The Ukraine war has underscored the importance of space as a domain for warfighting. When the USA restricted access to Starshield, for example, it immediately curtailed the ability of Ukrainian forces to target their Russian adversary.Also Watch: Indeed, a competition is occurring right now for ascendancy in space, and China represents the greatest threat to space-based activities of the USA and its allies.In late October 2026, the US Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) published a 130-page report entitled Challenges to Security in Space. Its purpose was to “provide an unclassified overview of the threats within the space domain that jeopardise US and allied national defence”.'I Was Unfaithful To My Wife': NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang Admits Extramarital Affair As Board Launches Independent Probe Into Reported China Spy Links This report was first published in 2019, with the next edition released in 2022. This therefore marks the third release of Challenges to Security in Space by the DIA.In its preamble, the 2026 report stated, “China, Russia, Iran and North Korea are developing, testing, deploying and using space capabilities in a way that threatens the security of all space systems and their associated space benefits.China and Russia are developing a formidable spectrum of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations. These countries have exhibited behaviours that often run counter to a safe, secure and sustainable space domain.”SpaceX Board Member Donald Harrison Resigns After 11 Years Amid Reported Tesla Merger Talks The report clearly identified the so-called CRINK nations – China, Russia, Iran and North Korea – as the main culprits. Furthermore, this quartet is intensifying and expanding its bilateral cooperation.“The malign efforts of these four actors go beyond the development of novel technology and extend into the diplomatic and economic arenas,” the DIA assessed.“China and Russia have proposed unverifiable international space treaties and commitments such as ‘no first placement of weapons in outer space’. Yet each refuses to acknowledge their ongoing efforts to develop dual-use and counterspace weaponry and their dangerous or ambiguous behaviour on-orbit.”Indeed, China receives the lion’s share of attention in the report. The section on Beijing’s activities stretched to 22 pages, whereas Russia garnered just 14 pages.India Clears 12 Electronics Component Manufacturing Applications With Over ₹7,500 Crore Proposed Investment In New Delhi It is noteworthy that China’s entire space programme is managed by the People’s Liberation Army (PLA), with the Central Military Commission (CMC) having oversight of both the PLA and the China National Space Administration.This contrasts with the USA, where military and civilian activities are separated into the Pentagon and NASA.The DIA claimed: “Beijing aims to become the pre-eminent leader in space, to shape international norms to be more supportive of China’s positions on space issues, and exploit other nations’ perceived reliance on space-based systems to deter and counter China’s military operations. China’s rapidly expanding space programme is second in size only to the US space programme: military, civil and commercial.”Anthropic's $1.5 Trillion IPO Faces Investor Pushback Amid AI Stock Selloff China has more than tripled its annual tally of space launches in the past decade. The country was responsible for 22 launches in 2016, a figure that reached 93 in 2025.That was a national record, and it included 25 commercial launches. By the same token, each launch now puts greater numbers of satellites into orbit on average.In 2016, China deployed 40 satellites, but this figure had reached 384 by last year.These satellites are used for intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR); communications; weapon targeting; meteorology; oceanography; and positioning, navigation and timing (PNT).As of mid-2026, China had more than 510 ISR satellites, a quantity that has tripled since 2018.Although many of these satellites are affiliated with commercial and civil missions, their dual-use nature means the data they collect can be used by the PLA.Temple Run: Eternal CEO Deepinder Goyal In Face-Off With Doctors Over Wearable Device The DIA stated, “China’s expansive system of ISR satellites can be used to support global monitoring, tracking and targeting of US and allied forces worldwide, especially throughout the Indo-Pacific region, including strategic locations such as the Korean Peninsula, Taiwan, the Philippines, the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea.”The document also accused Chinese ISR companies of supplying imagery to state actors banned by Western providers for supporting weapons proliferation.China’s burgeoning low Earth orbit (LEO) satellite constellation can provide images of any location in the world within 30 minutes.Its geostationary Earth orbit (GEO) signals intelligence, electro-optical and synthetic aperture radar satellites also provide coverage with no latency.Combined with other assets, the PLA can track objects anywhere in the Indo-Pacific region. This could include American aircraft carriers and expeditionary strike groups, for example.China is also exploring quantum-enabled communications, which would eventually ensure highly secure communications for the PLA.The BeiDou satellite navigation system is a blue-ribbon project for China. This instrument of national power offers worldwide coverage.Elon Musk Deletes Posts Urging Republican Votes After Democrats Win US Midterms BeiDou currently has 49 satellites in orbit to provide PNT services. The PLA relies on it for targeting by precision-guided weapons, for instance.Today, BeiDou has more than two billion users, including some countries that plan to use it as their primary PNT system, a state of affairs likely to lead to future dependencies on China.Beijing is getting its foot in the door with nations in Africa, Asia and Latin America via its Belt and Road Initiative.China provides training, joint development and launch of satellites, as well as services from its BeiDou satellite navigation system, for example.Alarmingly, the report noted: “China has developed and will continue to advance weapons for use against satellites in orbit to disrupt, damage and destroy other nations’ space capabilities.China continues to research, develop, test and deploy multiple types of counterspace weapons, including ground-based anti-satellite (ASAT) missile systems capable of destroying satellites.”In 2007, China infamously destroyed a defunct weather satellite using a missile.Also Watch: Later, in 2013, China launched an object to a range of 30,000km, which the DIA assesses was likely a missile capable of destroying satellites in GEO.The report noted, “To expand the range of its ASAT deterrent, China probably intends to deploy additional ASAT missiles that can destroy satellites in low, medium and high orbits.However, if ASAT missiles were used in a conflict, China would have to contend with the resulting large debris fields threatening its own on-orbit systems and those of neutral parties.”Alternatives to complete destruction are also available. Using ground-based and orbital systems, the PLA can jam adversary space systems during a conflict.Beijing can also use cyber operations to support military operations against satellites.The DIA suspects the Tongxin Jishu Shiyan series of satellites – of which there are now 27 – are capable of harming other satellites. On occasion, they have passed within 10km of foreign spacecraft.Furthermore, China is known to be researching space-based kinetic weapons that can be used against targets on the ground, at sea or in the air.China Warns Of Countermeasures After US Sanctions On Two Firms Over Cuba Ties The PLA can also use directed-energy weapons – such as lasers that can dazzle and temporarily blind sensors – against enemy space assets.These weapons can cause both reversible and irreversible effects against satellites.The DIA recorded: “China has multiple ground-based laser weapons with varying power levels to disrupt, degrade or damage satellites in LEO; by the late 2020s, China may field space-based directed-energy systems and higher-powered ground-based directed-energy systems capable of threatening satellites in higher orbits.”PLA doctrine consistently demonstrates an intention to control space-enabled information and to deny the domain’s use to enemies.Challenges to Security in Space 2026 summarised: “China’s development of a wide range of counterspace capabilities suggests the PLA probably is taking a combined-arms approach to space and seeks to threaten other nations’ satellites with multiple types of weapons.This combined-arms approach would enable the PLA to tailor its responses to particular situations, taking actions ranging from those that create temporary effects at the lowest level of escalation to actions that create permanent, non-reversible effects.PRC strategists very likely estimate that demonstrating counterspace capabilities during a crisis could threaten or incrementally degrade an adversary’s space architecture as a prelude to war.Hong Kong Activist Joshua Wong Sentenced To 10 Years In Prison For Conspiring To Seek Foreign Sanctions Against China PLA researchers assert that using space-related weapons to coerce a particular behaviour will have a lower threshold for use than nuclear weapons, and is a more controllable, flexible and credible option than nuclear deterrence, at least partially because these systems’ escalatory effects can also be modulated to disrupt, damage or destroy.”It continued, “China’s national military strategy emphasises the safeguarding of national sovereignty and territorial integrity as Beijing’s key objective and proclaims active defence – strategic defence paired with operational and tactical offence – as its guideline to contain and win wars.According to its national strategy and military literature, China identifies space as a strategic priority for military dominance and political influence.The Chinese military perceives space as a force multiplier that integrates cross-domain operations and platforms, an enabler of modern warfighting capabilities and a precondition for superiority and victories in other operational domains.”Hypocritically, China is pursuing agreements at the United Nations for the “non-weaponisation” of space.Yet, at the same time, Beijing is improving its counterspace weapons “to deter and compel other nations from taking actions Beijing deems counter to its national security interests,” the report accused.Taiwan clearly has military plans concerning Taiwan and, if an invasion or attack is carried out, the PLA would need to deter the USA from intervening.India Will Develop Its Own Tunnel-Boring Machines If China Halts Supply, Says Piyush Goyal Amid Export Curbs This reality is reflected in the report, which said, “The PLA probably sees counterspace operations as a way to dissuade and prevent an intervention from other nations during a regional military conflict.”Chairman Xi Jinping dissolved the Strategic Support Force of the PLA, which had been responsible for space operations, in April 2024.Those space capabilities were subsumed into the newly created Aerospace Force. This latter organisation falls directly under the CMC, giving immediate control to Xi and the top military body.Another aspect of developments in space is the growing dependence on commercial space capabilities for national security.As satellites become cheaper, smaller and faster to deploy, commercial enterprises are offering both state and non-state actors alternatives.Russia has targeted commercial constellations with jammers, particularly those from the USA. Furthermore, Moscow has increasingly looked to China for space-based support for its military operations against Ukraine.China has been pursuing a state-directed civil-military fusion policy designed to strengthen the PLA’s capability.China is now second only to the USA in terms of the amount of private capital being directed towards the space sector.Russia-Linked Hackers Used Compromised Websites To Steal Data From Unpatched iPhones & Android Phones: Cybersecurity Firm Says This is impressive, given that this explosion in commercial space companies has occurred in just a decade.Today, there are more than 400 Chinese companies ready to offer space services to both local and foreign clients.Looking into the future, the DIA report predicted: “China and Russia will continue to pursue new and improved counterspace capabilities to exploit a perceived US and allied reliance on space-based assets.China has developed and probably will continue to develop weapons for use against satellites in orbit to disrupt, damage and destroy adversary space capabilities.”The document’s writers also warned that both China and Russia will seek to compromise US space infrastructure to deny their strategic military, economic and political benefits.Furthermore, “Over the next decade, threats to systems, operations in space and the entire space domain could increase if China and Russia successfully develop reusable space systems and super-intelligence applications for space.”Super-intelligence, President Donald Trump’s preferred name for artificial intelligence, could expedite Chinese military capabilities and support actions against the USA and its allies during a conflict.What the report says, in a nutshell, is that the USA now has its hands full fending off Chinese efforts to diminish its dominance in space. news.title: World's largest climate summit COP31 opens as climate and geopolitical pressures mount
news.text:
ReutersA COP31 logo is pictured near the venue ahead of the United Nations climate change conference, known as COP31, in Antalya, Turkey

Antalya: The UN's annual climate talks kick off Monday in Turkey as rising temperatures heighten the urgency of action, with financial constraints and geopolitical tensions complicating efforts to secure global cooperation.More than 100,000 people are expected to attend COP31 in a sprawling expo centre in the Mediterranean seaside city of Antalya over the next two weeks.Negotiators from nearly 200 countries are facing tough discussions over how to accelerate the energy transition and provide funds to help developing nations cope with the worsening climate emergency.But observers say few major breakthroughs are expected as countries grapple with an oil price shock and geopolitical tensions fuelled by the US war with Iran and Russia's conflict in Ukraine.The climate emergency, meanwhile, continued to wreak havoc this year as punishing heatwaves baked Europe, wildfires raged in Indonesia and a glacier collapse triggered devastating floods in Nepal.Live EventsYou Might Also Like:COP31 gives India an opportunity to shape climate action, build coalition of developing nationsAn exceptionally strong El Nino climate phenomenon is forecast to peak later this year, adding to extreme weather and possibly helping to make 2026 or 2027 the hottest year on record.The outlook is bleak: the United Nations warned in September that global temperatures were on course to exceed 1.5C above preindustrial levels, breaching the most ambitious threshold set by the Paris Agreement."Global leaders must pull us back from the brink and commit to rapidly transitioning away from fossil fuels and expanding renewable energy, an imperative reinforced by the current energy affordability crisis," said Rachel Cleetus, climate programme director at the Union of Concerned Scientists.'Clean' electrification?Turkey is presiding over COP31, with Australia leading negotiations under an unusual arrangement that settled a dispute over who would host the conference.You Might Also Like:Climate finance, trade likely to be on COP31 tableThe partners have branded the summit as the "implementation COP", focusing on turning commitments into concrete action after years of pledges and ambitious announcements.Turkey is promoting an "action agenda" alongside the formal negotiations that encourages countries to support non-binding pledges on issues from artificial intelligence to waste management.Its centrepiece is an "electrification" drive to raise the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20 percent today to 35 percent by 2035.But the initiative could become a source of friction.The European Union has called for "clean" electrification, a term that could spark debate over the role of fossil fuels in the Turkish proposal.Countries committed to transition away from fossil fuels in a landmark pact at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 but have struggled to agree on how to turn that pledge into action.COP30 ended with a deal that made no explicit mention of fossil fuels after oil-producing countries opposed the language.Instead, Brazil produced a voluntary "roadmap" with proposals for phasing out fossil fuels that each country can tailor to their circumstances.Finance fightThe EU, for its part, and other developed countries are under pressure from the developing nations to fulfil promises to provide funds they need to adapt to climate impacts and recover from extreme weather disasters.A senior EU official warned that there would be "no political will" for extra funding pledges.African countries are pushing for the COP31 agenda to include discussions on the tripling of adaptation finance, which aims to help poorer nations pay for measures such as building sea walls or planting drought-resistant crops.Climate diplomacy is still missing a major player as President Donald Trump pulled the United States out of the Paris Agreement and has not sent officials to COP31.A US congressional delegation, however, will come to Antalya, with Democrats beaming after last week's historic US midterm election win.While negotiations are facing two weeks of gruelling talks, "the mood is very good", Azerbaijan's chief negotiator Yalchin Rafiyev told AFP.Countries need to turn "this positive spirit of being in a favourable environment into concrete, successful results", he said.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Trump says he was just kidding about making UFC's Dana White his press secretary
news.text:
WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. -- President Donald Trump said Sunday he was only kidding about making UFC boss Dana White his next White House press secretary after announcing on social media he had offered his close friend the job.

After his party's deep losses in Tuesday's midterm elections, Trump shook up his administration on Friday by replacing his chief of staff and followed up on Saturday with a post that said he had offered the press secretary job to White. On Sunday, Trump said it was "just a little fun."

"I was kidding, but I think Dana likes the idea, and he is a very capable guy," Trump said, speaking to reporters in Florida before departing for the White House. White is set to visit him at the White House on Monday.

The historic wins by Democratic candidates, including in areas that Republicans had held for decades, led to the GOP losing control of both chambers of Congress.

Trump on Friday named longtime aide Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles. Miller is the architect of the administration's hardline immigration policies. Trump does not currently have a press secretary after briefly giving the job to Katie Zacharia, who faltered behind the lectern and in interviews, and left the post after five days.
news.summary: President Donald Trump says he was only kidding about making UFC boss Dana White his next White House press secretary.

news.title: Nvidia announces probe into CEO Jensen Huang after he acknowledges affair with alleged Chinese spy
news.text:
Chip giant Nvidia’s board announced Sunday it opened a probe into Chief Executive and co-founder Jensen Huang after he acknowledged an affair with a woman US officials say was working for Chinese intelligence.

Late last month, The New York Times reported that US intelligence officials concluded that the woman, a Chinese executive linked to a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed, had been funnelling information to Beijing.

The executive, Alice Huang — also known as Huang Le, and no relation to 63-year-old Taiwanese-born Jensen Huang — developed a close relationship with the Nvidia boss, the Times said.

In a message to company employees released Sunday, Huang acknowledged having an affair and apologized to his family and company staff.

“I was unfaithful to my wife,” he said. “My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Jensen Huang is a huge figure in the artificial intelligence revolution and a close informal adviser to President Donald Trump, who has repeatedly spoken out against regulating the industry so as not to let China gain the upper hand in the AI race.

The Times said Huang’s relationship with the other Huang could have given her insights into Trump’s thinking around AI. The issue of AI is likely to arise during Trump’s planned talks with President Xi Jinping later this month at a summit in China.

Nvidia said in a statement it opened an independent probe “in light of recent reporting that founder and CEO Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort.”

The statement added: “While the Board has no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised, the Board’s inquiry will examine all available information.”

Asked about Huang on Sunday, Trump told reporters: “I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on. I’m sure — I hope everything’s fine. He’s done such an incredible job.”

The Chinese government has dismissed the Times report as “groundless speculation.”

‘Black eye moment’

China is in a race for tech dominance with the United States, which restricts the export to China of the most cutting-edge silicon chips.

Nvidia, a global leader in producing chips used to train and run AI models, is one of the world’s most valuable companies.

Megaspeed was under scrutiny for possibly steering Nvidia AI chips to China, the Times report said, citing unnamed sources briefed on the matter.

Trump was briefed on the intelligence findings about Huang’s relationship with the businesswoman roughly a year ago and chose not to act on the information, the Times report said.

Trump said Sunday he did not regret not acting on this intelligence. “No, I don’t think so. I think — you know, he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. You have to hear it.”

Technology analyst Dan Ives, with the investment bank Yorkville Ives, said word of the probe is “a black eye moment” for Jensen Huang.

Ives predicted it will at the very least spark multiple congressional inquiries and “create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons.”

In the near-term Huang is expected to keep his job but risks being removed as Nvidia’s CEO depending on the board’s probe, Ives said in a statement.

“This will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally,” he said. “This will also increase major scrutiny regarding selling chips to China, which remains a key battleground issue in DC.”

news.title: Leaders gather in Turkey for UN climate summit after a disastrous year of extreme weather
news.text:
ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — World leaders, delegates and climate activists on Monday will begin negotiations on curbing climate change, which in the last year has led to rising temperatures, deadly heat waves in Europe and beyond, and has played a role in disasters like the devastating floods in Nepal.

This U.N. climate summit, called the Conference of the Parties, or COP31, also comes as the war in Iran has effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, pushing up global prices of gasoline and oil and myriad products made with them, such as fertilizers and pesticides. The disruption has pushed governments to rethink energy policies, both in the short-term and long-term, including increased investment in renewable energy sources like wind and solar.

Delegates, meeting in the Turkish Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, will come under pressure to develop new pledges for climate action while implementing previous promises. The stakes are high: climate scientists say global average temperature rise will exceed 1.5 C (2.7 F) since the early 1800s.

Limiting temperature rise to that threshold was a goal established during the 2015 Paris Agreement. Since then, it’s been a focus of international climate negotiations. That the goal is no longer realistic underscores how difficult it’s been for the world to cut greenhouse gas emissions, which are released into the atmosphere when fossil fuels like oil, gas and coal are burned, leading to climate change.

“This is the first COP where it is clear beyond a reasonable doubt that the world will overshoot the 1.5-degree target,” said Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum. “We will not look away, and we will not lower our ambition.”

Kurum, the COP31 president, has said that rather than establishing new targets, he wants the summit to focus on turning previous climate commitments into action.

He has announced an “Action Agenda” that includes reducing methane, a greenhouse gas, and building climate-resilient cities, among other things. A central theme is electrification, with the aim of increasing the use of electricity — preferably from renewable energy such as solar and wind — from 21% to 35% by 2035, to reduce greenhouse emissions.

During the negotiations, scheduled Nov. 9-20, delegates are also expected to take up the issue of helping poorer countries pay to adapt to rising temperatures and extreme weather events, both tied to climate change, and transition away from fossil fuels.

The last two summits, COP30 in Brazil and COP29 in Azerbaijan, came under criticism for ending with little agreement on how to reduce greenhouse emissions. The final texts of those agreements didn’t even mention fuels; at COP28 in Dubai, delegates agreed to transition away from fossil fuels.

Undermining the summit, the United States, which is the world’s second-largest polluter after China, will again be absent. During his first term, and again when he took office for a second time in January 2025, President Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. from climate negotiations.

“No single COP is a silver bullet that can stop climate change overnight,” said U.N. Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell. “But every recent COP has made essential progress. COP31 in Antalya will, too.”

In a change from previous summits, COP31 is being jointly organized by Turkey and Australia after the two jostled over which would be the host. As a compromise, Turkey is the official host while Australia is leading the negotiations. However, both countries have come under criticism for their strong reliance on coal.
